lead: A photodiode turns light into current at a fixed rate. Quantum efficiency η counts how many incident photons yield collected electrons; responsivity R gives the current in amperes for each watt of light. Both connect an optical power in a fiber to the electrical signal a receiver sees. The idea exists because link design needs one number for the detector: microamperes per microwatt. It is used in specifying PIN and avalanche photodiodes, in receiver sensitivity budgets, and in choosing a wavelength for a given material. Only a few universities teach it as a separate topic; most fold it into the photodiode chapter.
prereq: You need Unit 3 on photon energy, bandgap and absorption, since η depends on how strongly the material absorbs at that wavelength.

sections.h3: Photon energy and the photon rate

blocks.text: A photon of wavelength λ carries energy E = hν = hc/λ. Here h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s is Planck's constant, ν is frequency in hertz, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s is the speed of light, and λ is in metres. At λ = 0.85 µm, E ≈ 2.34 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

Incident power P watts means P/E photons arrive every second. Facet reflection loses a fraction ρ; absorption depth, recombination and slow transit lose more. Quantum efficiency η is electrons collected per second divided by photons incident per second. It is a pure ratio, no units. A good antireflection coating raises η by lowering ρ.

Photons with energy below the bandgap E_g are not absorbed. So η falls to zero beyond the cutoff wavelength λ_c = 1.24/E_g, with λ_c in micrometres and E_g in electronvolts. This cutoff is a material property, not a circuit adjustment.
The primary photocurrent is set by how many collected electrons cross the junction each second. Responsivity is that current divided by the incident optical power.
I_ph = ηqP/hν = ηqPλ/(hc);  R = I_ph/P = ηλ/1.24
blocks.where: I_ph is photocurrent in A; η is quantum efficiency (no units); q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C is the electron charge; P is incident power in W; h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s; ν is frequency in Hz; λ is wavelength in µm for the last form; c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s; R is responsivity in A/W.

blocks.text: Because η ≤ 1, R ≤ λ/1.24 A/W. At 1.3 µm the ceiling is about 1.05 A/W; at 1.55 µm it is about 1.25 A/W. This is a hard ceiling set by photon energy, not by circuit design. Some syllabi treat quantum efficiency and responsivity as two separate marks.
The junction that collects these carriers is described in 4.2; gain in 4.3 multiplies this primary current.

figure.caption: Responsivity against wavelength for η = 1 and η = 0.8. The upper line is the hard ceiling; the lower line keeps the same shape and is scaled by 0.8.

spec.aria: Two straight lines of responsivity against wavelength in micrometres, one for quantum efficiency 1 and one for 0.8, both rising with wavelength and separated by a constant factor.

examples.question: A silicon PIN photodiode has η = 0.8 at λ = 0.85 µm and receives P = 1 µW. Find the photon arrival rate, the collected electron rate, the responsivity and the photocurrent.
steps: Collected electron rate N_e = ηN_p = 0.8 × 4.27 × 10¹² = 3.42 × 10¹² s⁻¹.
examples.answer: R ≈ 0.548 A/W, photon rate ≈ 4.28 × 10¹² s⁻¹, collected electron rate ≈ 3.42 × 10¹² s⁻¹, and I_ph ≈ 5.48 × 10⁻⁷ A.

traps: Using λ in metres in R = ηλ/1.24; the 1.24 shortcut needs λ in micrometres.
Treating η as A/W or R as a pure ratio; η has no units, R has A/W.
Claiming a better design can push R above λ/1.24; that is the η = 1 ceiling.
Assuming η = 1 by ignoring facet reflection and recombination.
Using R = ηλ/1.24 past the cutoff; beyond λ_c the material does not absorb, so R = 0.

quiz.a: η = electrons collected per second ÷ photons incident per second; it is a pure ratio.

quiz.q: Write the responsivity formula when λ is in micrometres.
Why can η have no units while R has A/W?
quiz.a: η counts particles per particle. R is current per optical power, so its units are C/s per W = A/W.

quiz.q: A detector has η = 0.9 at λ = 1.3 µm and P = 10 µW. Find R and I_ph.
At λ = 1.55 µm, P = 2 µW. Find the photon arrival rate.
Why is R = λ/1.24 an upper bound?
quiz.a: Each photon gives at most one collected electron, so η = 1 is the best case. The current per watt is then q/hν = qλ/hc = λ/1.24.

quiz.q: Why does R fall sharply to zero past the cutoff wavelength?
quiz.a: Photon energy drops below the bandgap, so interband absorption stops and no photoelectrons are collected.

beyond: Not for the exam. Waveguide photodetectors in silicon photonics increase absorption length without slowing transit, so η and bandwidth rise together. Balanced detection and coherent receivers use two photodiodes to cancel common noise; responsivity still sets the signal current. Foundry datacom receivers quote responsivity at 1.31 µm and 1.55 µm alongside dark current and bandwidth. Search next for waveguide photodetector, responsivity-bandwidth product, and quantum efficiency measurement.
